The reason is: In the case of any circle with a circumference of three handbreadths, there is a diameter of one handbreadth. But in the case of a square, one must have a perimeter of four handbreadths in order to have sides of one handbreadth. Since the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its perimeter is three to one, and the ratio of the perimeter of a square to its sides is four to one, the ratio of the circumference of a circle to the perimeter of a square is also three to four. Therefore, in order for a round sukkah to have a diameter of four cubits, its circumference must be twelve cubits. However, since the Sages required a square sukkah of four by four cubits, which has a perimeter of sixteen cubits, the circumference of a round sukkah must be correspondingly larger. According to this calculation, the circumference of a round sukkah would have to be sixteen cubits. Why, then, did Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai say that the circumference must be twenty-four cubits? The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai’s statement applies only when one wants the circumference of the circle to correspond to the perimeter of a square that circumscribes it, i.e., a square whose sides are equal to the diameter of the circle. In that case, the ratio of the circumference of the circle to the perimeter of the circumscribed square is three to four, so that a circle with a circumference of twenty-four cubits would be circumscribed by a square with a perimeter of thirty-two cubits. However, the Sages said that a sukkah is valid even if it is round, provided that it is large enough to contain a square of four by four cubits. In that case, the square is inscribed within the circle, and the ratio of the circumference of the circle to the perimeter of the inscribed square is not three to four. Rather, the circumference of the circle must be larger. According to the calculation of the Sages, a circle that can contain a square of four by four cubits has a circumference of sixteen and four-fifths cubits.
